result: The study was conducted in Balonghin, Burkina Faso, an area characterized by seasonal malaria transmission (August-December) with high falciparum parasite prevalence (>80% by 18S qPCR) during transmission season. Seasonal malaria chemoprophylaxis was not part of national guidelines at the time.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide well-documented contextual information about the study setting. The location, economic activities, and malaria transmission patterns are clearly stated with appropriate citations (C3, C4) to support the epidemiological characteristics of the area.

result: The study employed a comprehensive methodology including indoor mosquito collections at three timepoints (end 2013, start and peak 2014 transmission seasons), blood meal genotyping using microsatellite markers, mosquito speciation by PCR-RFLP, and parasite detection in both humans (18S qPCR, Pfs25 mRNA qRT-PCR) and mosquitoes (nested PCR).
evaluation: Claims C6-C25 describe well-established methodological approaches with appropriate citations to published protocols. The methods are clearly described and use validated techniques for mosquito collection, DNA extraction, genotyping, and parasite detection.

result: The study included 35 households with median 3 individuals per household. High bed net use (88.1%) was reported. At enrollment, 79.2% of individuals were parasite-positive, with all individuals infected in 21/35 houses. Collections yielded 325, 620, and 190 bloodfed mosquitoes at start, peak, and end of transmission season respectively, with significantly higher daily collection rates at start and peak compared to end (p≤0.001).
evaluation: Claims C26-C40 provide clear descriptive statistics with appropriate statistical comparisons. The data on household characteristics, parasite prevalence, and mosquito collection numbers are well-documented and internally consistent across the manuscript and Table 1.

result: Of 1,135 collected mosquitoes, 93.9% had blood meals analyzed successfully. After excluding 100 failed amplifications, 153 multiple-source meals, and 139 unmatched meals, 68.9% (666/966) of typed blood meals were used for exposure estimates. Approximately 20% of individuals provided 85.1%, 76.0%, and 95.5% of single mosquito blood meals at start, peak, and end of transmission season respectively.
evaluation: Claims C41-C48 document the data processing pipeline and demonstrate extreme heterogeneity in mosquito exposure exceeding the Pareto rule (20/80) in two of three surveys. The proportions are clearly stated and consistent with Figure 1, providing strong evidence for the main finding.

result: A small number of individuals, mostly adults, received considerably higher numbers of mosquito bites compared to the rest of the population. Conversely, 32.0-76.2% of participants were not linked to any bloodfed mosquitoes, including 15/77 individuals present in all surveys. Bed net use, parasite carriage, and gametocyte carriage at enrollment were not significantly associated with mosquito exposure (all p>0.05).
evaluation: Claims C49-C54 describe the distribution of mosquito exposure with appropriate statistical testing. The lack of association with bed net use and infection status is clearly stated with confidence intervals and p-values, though the study acknowledges it was not designed to assess these factors.

result: Negative binomial regression better explained mosquito bite distribution than Poisson models (p<0.001) after adjusting for age, survey, and household correlation. Sensitivity analyses assigning multiple-source blood meals to least exposed individuals still showed ~20% of population received ≥70% of bites. Alternative analysis using genetic distance assignment yielded similar patterns (78.6%, 76.3%, 94.2% at start, peak, end).
evaluation: Claims C55-C60 demonstrate appropriate statistical modeling with model comparison and sensitivity analyses. The overdispersion finding is well-supported, and multiple analytical approaches converge on similar conclusions about heterogeneity, strengthening the robustness of the main result.

result: For individuals in all surveys, positive correlations existed between mosquito exposure at start-peak (r=0.24, p=0.04) and start-end (r=0.34, p=0.002) of transmission season, suggesting some consistency in preferential biting. However, some highly exposed individuals at peak received few or no bites in other surveys.
evaluation: Claims C61-C64 provide statistical evidence for temporal patterns in exposure with appropriate correlation analyses. The finding of both consistency and variability is well-documented with Figure 2a providing visual support for individual-level temporal variation.

result: Within-household heterogeneity was observed: in households with ≥3 participants and ≥5 matched mosquitoes, the most exposed individual provided ≥50% of blood meals in 4/8, 14/15, and 7/7 households at start, peak, and end respectively. While highly exposed individuals often lived in high-mosquito households, all houses had individuals with relatively low exposure.
evaluation: Claims C65-C70 document within-household heterogeneity with clear criteria for inclusion and specific proportions. Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 provide visual support. The finding that heterogeneity exists at both household and individual levels is well-demonstrated.

result: Mosquito species composition varied seasonally: A. coluzzii represented 44.7% at start, while A. gambiae s.s. dominated at peak (74.0%) and end (53.7%). A. coluzzii had higher rates of multiple-source blood meals (18.9-22.0% vs 10.3-16.1%). Negative binomial models better fit species-specific bite distributions with significant overdispersion parameters (A. coluzzii: 1.9, 95% CI 1.2-3.2; A. gambiae s.s.: 2.5, 95% CI 1.8-3.6). Exposure to different species was positively associated (all p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C71-C79 provide comprehensive species-specific analysis with appropriate statistical modeling. The overdispersion finding for both species and positive association between exposures support the conclusion that heterogeneity occurs irrespective of vector species, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

result: Malaria parasite prevalence in bloodfed mosquitoes was 23.4%, 4.9%, and 8.0% at end, start, and peak of transmission season respectively, and slightly higher in singly-matched versus multiple-source mosquitoes. A. coluzzii mosquitoes were less often infected than A. gambiae s.s. (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.22-0.76).
evaluation: Claims C80-C84 present infection prevalence data with appropriate statistical analysis (Table 2). The species difference in infection rates is well-documented with odds ratios and confidence intervals from mixed effects logistic regression adjusted for survey timing.

result: Only 7.7%, 23.6%, and 10.5% of subjects were linked to potentially infectious mosquito meals at start, peak, and end respectively. The two most exposed individuals in each survey experienced 44-50% of all infectious bites. Total mosquito exposure positively predicted infectious bites (p<0.001). Household-level clustering of infectious bites was observed (ICC 0.19, 95% CI 0.08-0.38, p<0.001) but no individual-level clustering after adjusting for household (p=0.50).
evaluation: Claims C85-C91 demonstrate extreme concentration of infectious bite exposure with appropriate multilevel statistical modeling. The finding of household but not individual clustering conditional on total bites is well-supported by mixed effects models, though the biological mechanisms remain speculative.

result: The observed mosquito biting heterogeneity could increase malaria R0 by ≥3-fold compared to random mixing. Specifically, R0 increased by factors of 4.8, 4.2, and 8.4 at start, peak, and end of transmission season. Conservative sensitivity analysis still yielded R0 increases of 3.3, 3.2, and 5.7 respectively.
evaluation: Claims C92-C98 apply established theoretical frameworks (cited to Smith et al., 2007; Churcher et al., 2015) to calculate R0 inflation. While the mathematical approach is sound and sensitivity analyses are provided, the authors acknowledge important limitations: the framework doesn't account for finite population effects, immunity interactions, or spatial dependencies. The R0 calculations represent theoretical upper bounds rather than empirically validated transmission impacts.

result: The distribution of mosquito bites exceeded the Pareto rule (20/80) in two of three surveys (20/85, 20/96), with maximum heterogeneity estimated to inflate malaria R0 by 8-fold. Distribution of sporozoite-positive bites followed similar patterns. Heterogeneity in mosquito exposure contributes considerably to heterogeneity in infection risk and suggests significant variation in malaria transmission potential.
evaluation: Claims C99-C103 summarize the main findings from the abstract. The extreme heterogeneity in both total and infectious bites is well-documented throughout the manuscript with multiple lines of evidence. However, the R0 inflation estimate (C100) should be interpreted cautiously given the theoretical limitations acknowledged in the Discussion.

result: Malaria epidemiology depends on frequency and efficiency of human-mosquito contacts. Individuals within the same locality may not be equally likely to be bitten, with exposure influenced by host availability and attractiveness. More than three-quarters of exposure occurs indoors, with age and body surface area as major determinants of attractiveness. Previous work by the authors showed mosquitoes in this area fed more often on adults.
evaluation: Claims C104-C109 provide appropriate background context with citations to relevant literature. These claims establish the scientific rationale for the study and are well-supported by prior research, including the authors' previous work (C109).

result: At peak transmission, the highest-mosquito household had ~150 times more fed mosquitoes than the lowest. Household characteristics (construction, windows, eaves, proximity to breeding sites) are known to affect indoor exposure. A Kenya study showed malaria foci are unstable with limited predictive value over time. Consistent with this, household ranking by infected bites varied over time, and within-household differences reached up to 51 matched meals (≈10 bites/day) at peak.
evaluation: Claims C110-C114 document between- and within-household variation with specific quantitative data. The temporal instability finding (C113) is supported by Figure 3 and appropriately contextualized with citation to similar findings from Kenya (C112). The extreme within-household variation (C114) is clearly stated.

result: Blood meals from 8.2% of mosquitoes did not amplify for human DNA. Analyses used ~70% of successfully typed meals. Of unmatched meals, 139/292 were single meals from non-residents and 153/292 had multiple sources. Genetic profiles of unmatched meals suggest heterogeneous feeding: in three houses with >10 unmatched mosquitoes, 16/41, 8/13, and 31/33 meals had the same profile.
evaluation: Claims C115-C119 transparently acknowledge study limitations regarding incomplete data usage. The authors appropriately discuss potential biases and provide data on unmatched meals. The heterogeneous feeding pattern inference (C119) is supported by the genetic profile data, though the biological interpretation remains somewhat speculative.

result: Broad differences in anthropophily between mosquito species are well-recognized, but fewer data exist on species-specific feeding preferences for individual humans. Despite seasonal species abundance differences, aggregation in human biting occurred irrespective of species, with exposure to one species positively associated with others. Evidence from Senegal suggests A. gambiae s.s. may be more susceptible to infection, though not consistently observed. The higher infection frequency in A. gambiae s.s. confirms its prime importance for transmission in this setting.
evaluation: Claims C120-C124 appropriately contextualize the species-specific findings with relevant literature. The conclusion about A. gambiae s.s. importance (C124) is well-supported by the infection data (C84) and abundance data (C71-C73), though the mechanistic explanation for species differences remains uncertain.

result: Mosquitoes with multiple blood meals are more likely to infect multiple individuals per night. Species composition varies during the rainy season, potentially impacting infection propagation rates. Between 75-90% of participants were not matched to infected mosquitoes. Blood meal genotyping with sporozoite assessment could improve understanding of clinical malaria risk heterogeneity. Household-level clustering of infectious bites was not related to local mosquito abundance, possibly linked to limited mosquito-human mixing or local factors affecting mosquito survival and age.
evaluation: Claims C125-C131 present logical inferences and speculative mechanisms. While the observation of household clustering independent of abundance (C129) is data-supported, the proposed mechanisms (C130) are explicitly speculative with appropriate citations but lack direct empirical validation in this study. The suggestion for future research (C128) is reasonable but represents a proposal rather than a demonstrated result.

result: Only limited data are available for natural Anopheles exposure. The findings show significant heterogeneity consistent with the 20/80 rule and support designing interventions targeting a small proportion of the population. Opportunities for targeting high-exposure households depend on operational feasibility to identify them and stability of exposure over time.
evaluation: Claims C132-C134 appropriately contextualize the study's contribution and discuss implications for intervention design. The support for targeted interventions (C133) follows logically from the heterogeneity findings, though the practical challenges (C134) are appropriately acknowledged given the temporal instability observed.

result: Ethical clearance was obtained from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine ethics committee (reference 6447) and the ethical review committee of the Ministry of Health of Burkina Faso (2013-7-58).
evaluation: Claims C135-C136 document appropriate ethical approvals from both UK and Burkina Faso institutions with specific reference numbers, meeting standard requirements for human subjects research.
